claim: Article 368(1): Parliament may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by addition, variation or repeal any provision of the Constitution, by the procedure in the article.

claim: Article 368(2): an amendment is started only by a Bill in either House; it needs a majority of the total membership of that House AND not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting; then the President shall give assent (cannot send it back).
value: majority of total membership + 2/3 of present and voting, each House; President shall assent
source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27

claim: Article 368 proviso: if the amendment changes certain provisions it must also be ratified by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before it goes to the President.

second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27

claim: The 24th Amendment Act received assent on 5 Nov 1971. Its Statement of Objects says Golaknath had, by a narrow majority, reversed earlier decisions, and the Act makes explicit that Parliament can amend any provision including Part III.
source: Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, Legislative Department
page_or_section: Statement of Objects and Reasons; ss.2-3
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Act inserted Art. 13(4), Art. 368(1) and (3), and made the President's assent to an amendment Bill compulsory.

claim: The 25th Amendment Act (assent 20 Apr 1972) replaced 'compensation' by 'amount' in Art. 31(2), made Art. 19(1)(f) inapplicable to such laws, and inserted Art. 31C for laws giving effect to Art. 39(b) or (c).
source: Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, Legislative Department
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Court's own Kesavananda headnote (PDF p.3-4) describes the same. Note the Act is called 1971 but assent was in 1972.

claim: The 29th Amendment Act (assent 9 Jun 1972) put the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Acts of 1969 and 1971 in the Ninth Schedule (entries 65, 66).
source: Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972, Legislative Department
second_source: Waman Rao v Union of India, (1981) 2 SCC 362 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Statement of Objects names it the '(Thirty-second Amendment) Bill, 1972' that was enacted as the 29th Act: Bill numbers and Act numbers differ.

claim: The 39th Amendment Act (assent 10 Aug 1975) inserted Article 329A (special provision for elections of the Prime Minister and Speaker), took election disputes of President and Vice-President out of the courts, and added Acts to the Ninth Schedule.
source: Constitution (Thirty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1975, Legislative Department
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: The 44th Amendment later omitted Art. 329A (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).

claim: The 42nd Amendment Act (assent 18 Dec 1976): s.4 widened Art. 31C to 'all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV'; s.55 added Art. 368(4) and (5).
source: Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, Legislative Department
second_source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Its own Statement of Objects (para 3) says directive principles are to have precedence over those fundamental rights that were 'allowed to be relied upon' against reforms; para 4 says it wants to put the amending power 'beyond doubt'.

claim: The 42nd Amendment also extended the term of the House of the People and State Assemblies from five to six years (and Art. 371F in the same way).
source: Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, Legislative Department
second_source: NCERT Politics in India since Independence (Class XII), ch. 6, Reprint 2026-27
note: The 44th Amendment restored five years (not read at Act level; see A10 caveat). Belongs mainly to POL-07 (Emergency).

claim: The 43rd Amendment Act (assent 13 Apr 1978) omitted Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A, 228A and 31D, which the 42nd Amendment had added to curb judicial review.
source: Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, Legislative Department
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
note: These articles required larger benches and special majorities (two-thirds) to strike down a law. NCERT p.210 describes the restoration in general terms only.

claim: The Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014 inserted Article 124A (the National Judicial Appointments Commission); the Supreme Court declared it, and the NJAC Act 2014, unconstitutional and void on 16 Oct 2015.
source: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India, WP(C) 13 of 2015 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: Order of the Court, items 2-3 (signed by all five); para 568 of the lead text (author not pinned in the re-host)

claim: Shankari Prasad (decided 5 Oct 1951, five-judge bench): the Court upheld the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 (which inserted Arts 31A and 31B) and held 'law' in Art. 13(2) means ordinary legislation, not a constitutional amendment.
source: Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v Union of India, [1952] SCR 89 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Bench named in the header: Patanjali Sastri, Kania CJ, Mukherjea, Das, Aiyar. The court's own Kesavananda headnote confirms 'unanimously'.

claim: Sajjan Singh (decided 30 Oct 1964, five-judge bench): the Court upheld the 17th Amendment (which added 44 Acts to the Ninth Schedule) and declined to reconsider Shankari Prasad; three judges formed the majority.
source: Sajjan Singh v State of Rajasthan, [1965] 1 SCR 933 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: headnote 'HELD (by P.B. Gajendragadkar C.J., Wanchoo, and Raghubar Dayal JJ.)'
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: All five agreed the petitions fail. Hidayatullah and Mudholkar JJ. kept the 13(2) question open ('quaere').

claim: In Sajjan Singh, Mudholkar J. asked whether changing a basic feature of the Constitution could count as an 'amendment' at all, but said it was doubt, not a final view. This is the earliest seed of the doctrine in the cases read.
source: Sajjan Singh v State of Rajasthan, [1965] 1 SCR 933 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: Mudholkar J., SCR pp.966-967 (text lines on 'basic features')
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Do not call this 'the first' without checking cases before 1964 (UNVERIFIED as to priority). Quote shown as in re-host; scan errors in the word 'indicate'.

claim: Golaknath (decided 27 Feb 1967, eleven-judge bench, 6:5): an amendment is 'law' under Art. 13(2); Parliament could not take away or abridge Part III rights by amendment; Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh were overruled for the future (prospective overruling) so the 1st, 4th and 17th Amendments stood.
source: I.C. Golaknath v State of Punjab, [1967] 2 SCR 762 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Majority: Subba Rao CJ, Shah, Sikri, Shelat, Vaidialingam, with Hidayatullah concurring. Dissent: Wanchoo, Bachawat, Ramaswami, Bhargava, Mitter. Result on the facts: petitions dismissed (17th Amendment saved).

claim: Kesavananda Bharati was decided on 24 Apr 1973 by a thirteen-judge Constitution Bench (Writ Petition 135 of 1970 and connected petitions); the Record of Proceedings lists the 13 judges and the court's order.
source: Record of Proceedings 24 Apr 1973, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Bench: Sikri CJ, Shelat, Hegde, Grover, Ray, P. Jaganmohan Reddy, Palekar, Khanna, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, Mukherjea, Chandrachud. The ROP scan is poor OCR; the names are confirmed on the SCR title page.

claim: The challenge began against the Kerala Land Reforms Amendment Acts of 1969 and 1971; while it was pending, the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments were passed and also challenged.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Constitution (Twenty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1972, Legislative Department

claim: The Court gave eleven separate judgments (Sikri CJ; Shelat and Grover jointly; Hegde and Mukherjea jointly; and Ray, Jaganmohan Reddy, Palekar, Khanna, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, Chandrachud each alone).
source: Record of Proceedings 24 Apr 1973, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Count is mine from the Record of Proceedings and the SCR layout (1+1+1+8). The Record text is garbled by OCR; names match the SCR.

claim: Holding on the core question: by 7 to 6, the power to amend does not include the power to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution so as to change its identity. For: Sikri CJ, Shelat, Hegde, Grover, Khanna, Jaganmohan Reddy, Mukherjea. Against: Ray, Palekar, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, Chandrachud.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
page_or_section: SCR headnote (PDF p.4), 'By majority: Per Sikri, C.J. and Shelat...'
note: Court's own SCR headnote. The Court's explainer page (Intro/Conclusion) also says 7-6. IMPORTANT: 7:6 counts judges on this one question. On other questions the majorities are different (see D05-D08), so 'a 7-6 verdict' is only true of this question. Count is the SCR reporter's headnote, same publisher as the Court's explainer page (which also says 7-6), so not independent; explainer dropped as second source. Signed summary has 9 signatures (D09). Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: By a majority of ten (Hegde, Ray, Jaganmohan Reddy, Palekar, Khanna, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, Mukherjea, Chandrachud) the Golaknath view that 'law' in Art. 13(2) covers constitutional amendments is erroneous and overruled.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Sikri CJ treated the Golaknath question as academic and did not decide it. Summary item 1 signed by nine says 'Golak Nath's case is over-ruled'.

claim: By 7 to 6 (Ray, Palekar, Khanna, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, Chandrachud; against: Sikri, Shelat, Hegde, Grover, Mukherjea; Jaganmohan Reddy left it open) there are no inherent or implied limitations on the amending power. Khanna J. is in the 7-judge group on both counts, so the two groups of seven overlap but are not the same people.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Why '7:6' is shorthand. Khanna's own paragraph (SCR p.50): plenary power including fundamental rights, subject to retaining the basic structure or framework.

claim: On Art. 31C as inserted by the 25th Amendment: a majority held the first part valid and the second part (no court may question a law carrying a declaration that it gives effect to the policy) invalid. Sikri CJ, Shelat, Hegde, Grover, Mukherjea held both parts invalid; Ray, Palekar, Mathew, Beg, Dwivedi, Chandrachud held both valid; Jaganmohan Reddy and Khanna held the first valid (Reddy with words severed) and the second invalid.
value: first part valid, second part invalid
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Result used later: Waman Rao and Minerva Mills treat the 'unamended' Art. 31C (first part) as valid.

claim: By the full Court: the 24th Amendment, s.2(a) and (b) of the 25th Amendment, and the 29th Amendment are valid.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Second source is the signed 'view of the majority' items 3, 4 and 6 (PDF p.1005). So the petitioners lost on the amendments they attacked and still won the doctrine.

claim: The court's signed 'view by the majority' has six numbered items; item 2 reads that Art. 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution. It is signed by nine judges (Sikri, Shelat, Hegde, Grover, Jaganmohan Reddy, Palekar, Khanna, Mukherjea, Chandrachud). Ray, Mathew, Beg and Dwivedi did not sign it; all thirteen signed the order.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Note: two of the nine signers (Palekar, Chandrachud) are shown by the headnote as dissenting on the basic-structure question, so the 9-signature summary and the 7:6 count are different ways of counting. How to reconcile this is a scholars' debate (see D10).

claim: The status of the signed summary was disputed inside the Supreme Court itself: in Minerva Mills (1980) Chandrachud CJ said, whatever its formal status, it 'correctly reflects the majority view'; in the same case Bhagwati J. said it has no legal effect and cannot be law declared under Art. 141, but held himself bound by the common ratio extracted by a five-judge bench.
source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: Chandrachud CJ (majority) and Bhagwati J. opinions
second_source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Both views are in one judgment. The Court's own site lists scholars (Andhyarujina; Minattur 'The Ratio in the Kesavananda Bharati Case', 1974) on this; those were not read. State as a disagreement, not as settled.

claim: Sikri CJ's list in Kesavananda: supremacy of the Constitution; republican and democratic form of government; secular character; separation of powers among legislature, executive and judiciary; federal character; resting on the dignity and freedom of the individual.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Bhagwati J. in Minerva Mills (not the majority opinion)

claim: Shelat and Grover JJ. gave a six-item list: supremacy of the Constitution; republican democratic form and sovereignty; secular and federal character; demarcation of power among legislature, executive, judiciary; dignity of the individual (Part III) with the mandate to build a welfare State (Part IV); unity and integrity of the nation.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Bhagwati J., Minerva Mills lines 4168-4170 (his paraphrase; adds 'justice' that the headnote list does not carry)
note: They call it 'illustrating'. CONFIRMED for the headnote list only. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: Hegde and Mukherjea JJ. listed sovereignty of India, democratic character of the polity, unity of the country, essential features of individual freedoms, and the mandate to build a welfare State and egalitarian society, and said the limits are 'only illustrative and not exhaustive'.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Lokur J. (concurring with the 4:1 majority), NJAC, quoting Kesavananda
note: Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: Jaganmohan Reddy J. drew the elements from the Preamble: sovereign democratic republic; justice (social, economic, political); liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; equality of status and opportunity; and said parliamentary democracy and the three organs of the State 'certainly' form part of it.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Bhagwati J., Minerva Mills lines 4172-4177
note: Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: Khanna J. gave no list in the headnote; his holding is that the amending power does not include power to abrogate the Constitution or alter its basic structure or framework. Bhagwati J. in Minerva Mills says Khanna J. treated the right to property as a matter of detail and 'appeared to be of the view' that democratic form, secular character and judicial review are part of the structure.
value: no list; Bhagwati J.'s hedged reading
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Bhagwati J., Minerva Mills lines 4177-4182 (separate opinion, not the majority)

claim: Bhagwati J.'s separate opinion in Minerva Mills (1980), not the majority opinion of Chandrachud CJ, says: the Kesavananda majority did not lay down that any named features form the basic structure; the six judges' lists were illustrations with no binding authority (obiter, merely illustrative, and not a majority opinion); and in every case the question turns on the feature's place in the scheme, its object and purpose, and the effect of denying it on the Constitution's integrity. For that test he cites Chandrachud J. in Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain, p.658.
value: no single binding list; case-by-case test

source: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, [1976] 2 SCR 347 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: Chandrachud J. para 696 (clauses (4) and (5) void); Khanna 213 and Mathew 343 (clause (4) void); Ray CJ 62-65; Beg 636 (cl.(4) does not bar the appeals); appeal allowed Ray 158, Khanna 254, Mathew 386, Beg 636
second_source: Waman Rao v Union of India, (1981) 2 SCC 362 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: The judges gave different reasons: Khanna J. struck down cl.(4) because free and fair elections, part of democracy, are basic structure; Ray CJ treated cl.(4) as Parliament exercising judicial power without applying law, and doubted that free and fair election is a 'basic structure' (para 51-52 region, text partly truncated in the re-host). Do not say 'the Court held X is basic structure' without naming the judge. Para 696 is the last paragraph of Chandrachud J.'s concurring opinion, not Beg J.'s; Beg J. does not say void. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: Mathew J. in Indira Gandhi: the Kesavananda majority limit applies to the amending power; he found no such inhibition on ordinary legislation by Parliament or State legislatures, which are tested against the Constitution's specific provisions. Ray CJ likewise rejects applying basic-structure limits to ordinary laws.
value: doctrine applies to amendments, not ordinary laws
source: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, [1976] 2 SCR 347 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: Mathew J. paras 344-346; Ray CJ paras 132-134
second_source: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India, WP(C) 13 of 2015 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Second source (Goel J. in NJAC) assumes the doctrine may not apply to statutes and tests the NJAC Act under Arts 14, 19, 21 instead.

claim: Common belief: 'Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain was the first time a constitutional amendment was struck down'. Correction: in Kesavananda (1973) the Court had already held the second part of s.3 of the 25th Amendment (the part inserting Art. 31C's bar on questioning declarations) invalid, so an amendment provision was struck two years earlier.
source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
second_source: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain, [1976] 2 SCR 347 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Rule: avoid 'first/only' claims. Safe wording: 'In 1975 the Court struck down clauses of the 39th Amendment itself.'

claim: Minerva Mills (decided 31 Jul 1980, five-judge bench): s.55 of the 42nd Amendment (Art. 368(4) and (5)) was held void by all five judges; s.4 of the 42nd Amendment (amended Art. 31C) was held void by four (Chandrachud CJ, Gupta, Untwalia, Kailasam) with Bhagwati J. dissenting on that point, who held amended Art. 31C valid.
source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
note: Bhagwati J.'s statement: he would declare s.55 void and amended Art. 31C valid. Headnote labels him 'concurring' though he dissents on 31C; read his operative lines, not the label.

claim: Minerva Mills: the majority held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot enlarge it into an absolute power ('The power to destroy is not a power to amend'); and that the balance between Part III and Part IV is an essential feature of the basic structure.
source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
note: The 'two wheels of a chariot' image is in the headnote.

claim: Waman Rao (judgment 13 Nov 1980; short order of 9 May 1980; five-judge bench): Arts 31A and unamended 31C valid; laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before 24 Apr 1973 keep Art. 31B protection; those placed on or after 24 Apr 1973 are valid only if they do not damage or destroy the basic structure.
source: Waman Rao v Union of India, (1981) 2 SCC 362 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
second_source: I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu, (2007) 2 SCC 1 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Minerva's last page refers to 'the order dated 9th May 1980 in Waman Rao's case' and says reasons will come later.

claim: I.R. Coelho (decided 11 Jan 2007, nine-judge bench, judgment delivered by Sabharwal CJI): Ninth Schedule laws put in after 24 Apr 1973 can be challenged if they destroy or damage the basic structure; the test is the effect on rights (the 'rights test' and 'essence of the right' test), judged with Art. 21 read with Arts 14 and 19; the cases then go to three-judge benches.
source: I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu, (2007) 2 SCC 1 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
second_source: Waman Rao v Union of India, (1981) 2 SCC 362 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: The re-host does not show whether any judge wrote separately. Nine-judge bench named in the header: Sabharwal CJI, Bhan, Pasayat, B.P. Singh, Kapadia, Thakker, Balasubramanyan, Kabir, D.K. Jain.

claim: NJAC case (decided 16 Oct 2015, five-judge bench): by 4 to 1 the 99th Amendment (Art. 124A and the NJAC) was struck down as altering the basic structure through the independence of the judiciary; the NJAC Act was also struck down; the collegium system was declared operative; the plea to reconsider the Second and Third Judges cases was rejected. Chelameswar J. would have upheld the Amendment.
source: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India, WP(C) 13 of 2015 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: Order of the Court; Chelameswar J. para 120; Lokur J. para 3 (agrees with Khehar, Joseph, Goel on the 99th Amendment; disagrees with Chelameswar); para 568-569 of the lead text (author not pinned)
second_source: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v Union of India, WP(C) 13 of 2015 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: Chelameswar J. also signed the Court's order; his written reasons are the dissent. The 4:1 count is mine from the text of the five opinions (the re-host merges them).

claim: Property Owners Association v State of Maharashtra (decided 5 Nov 2024, nine-judge bench): Art. 31C to the extent upheld in Kesavananda Bharati remains in force; the Court held the unamended Art. 31C was revived when Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's s.4.
source: Property Owners Association v State of Maharashtra, 2024 INSC 835 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
page_or_section: CJI Chandrachud's opinion, Conclusion para 229(a); paras 70-71
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: Seven judges signed the main opinion; the other two judges wrote separately (not summarised here). Matters in the reference were sent back to a regular bench.

claim: On 17 Sep 1949 Dr Ambedkar moved the draft Article 304 (amendment procedure); the Assembly adopted draft Article 304 as amended that day.
source: Constituent Assembly Debates Vol IX, 17 Sep 1949 (third-party mirror; Parliament's copy unreachable)
page_or_section: CAD Vol. IX, 17 Sep 1949 (mirror paragraph numbers 9.143.451-452; adoption just before 9.143.623)
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Mirror is not Parliament's copy; the court's headnote (Khanna J.) independently refers to the 17 Sep 1949 speech.

claim: Ambedkar explained three groups of articles: those amendable by Parliament by simple majority (e.g. arts 2 and 3 on States), those needing a two-thirds majority, and a small set needing two-thirds plus ratification by the States because they concern Centre-State relations.
source: Constituent Assembly Debates Vol IX, 17 Sep 1949 (third-party mirror; Parliament's copy unreachable)
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Khanna J.'s headnote summarises the same three categories.

claim: Ambedkar said that, among the Constitutions he cited (Canada, Ireland, Switzerland, Australia, USA), none lets the Constitution be amended by a simple majority.
source: Constituent Assembly Debates Vol IX, 17 Sep 1949 (third-party mirror; Parliament's copy unreachable)
note: Single mirror source for the speech; check at Parliament's copy before quoting.

claim: Ambedkar, 25 Nov 1949: if those dissatisfied with the Constitution cannot even get a two-thirds majority in a Parliament elected on adult franchise, their dissatisfaction cannot be deemed shared by the general public. NCERT cites this as CAD Vol. XI p.976.
source: Constituent Assembly Debates Vol XI, 25 Nov 1949 (third-party mirror; Parliament's copy unreachable)
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
note: Mirror only; Parliament's copy not reached. NCERT page 203.

claim: NCERT (Class XI, ch.9, p.211) says the Kesavananda ruling (1973): sets limits on amending power, still lets Parliament amend any part within the limit, and makes the judiciary the final authority on whether an amendment violates the basic structure.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
note: Matches the court's holding (Khanna J. at SCR p.50 and signed item 2). The third point (judiciary as final authority) is NCERT's inference from the judgment; it follows from judicial review but is not a numbered holding.

claim: NCERT says 'the theory was accepted by all institutions for four decades' and that the Venkatachaliah Commission (2000) did not suggest anything endangering the basic structure.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
note: The commission's report was not read (Government of India). NCERT only.

claim: NCERT p.215: after Kesavananda, attempts were made to ask the Court to reconsider; when they failed the 42nd amendment asserted parliamentary supremacy; the Court repeated its stand in Minerva Mills (1980).
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
second_source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: The review bench (reconsideration of Kesavananda, 1975) was not read; only NCERT and the 42nd Act's own Statement of Objects support the 'attempt to override' reading.

claim: NCERT Class XI p.202 works the two-part special majority with a Lok Sabha of 545 and a minimum of 273 votes. Correction: 545 included two nominated Anglo-Indian members; NCERT's own 2024 revision note gives 543 as the Lok Sabha's total membership after the 104th Amendment, which would make the 'at least half' figure 272. Art. 81 caps elected seats at 530 + 20.
source: NCERT Revised and Updated Content in Social Sciences, Political Science (2024)
page_or_section: Class VIII Social and Political Life III, ch.3, item 3(iii) (the note is in a different book); Constitution Art. 81(1)
second_source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
note: Second source for the present strength (sansad.in / ECI) not read: UNVERIFIED. Also leaves open how vacancies affect 'total membership' (not settled in sources read). Do not state 272 on screen without that check; safer to teach the rule, not the number.

claim: NCERT Class XI p.205 says the Constitution 'has been amended 106 times' as of 26 Jan 2024 (74 years). This matches the Legislative Department's count (106 Amendment Acts as of 10 Sep 2026). The same chapter's opening still says 'the last 69 years' (p.196-197).
value: 106; chapter uses 69 and 74 years in different places
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27
second_source: Constitution of India as on 10 Sep 2026, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice
note: NCERT's 2024 revision list says the update was deliberately made in two places (p.205, 207) and not in p.196-197; the chapter is internally inconsistent on years. Always quote the year with the count.

claim: NCERT Class XI ch.6 (Judiciary) p.142 says the Kesavananda Court 'ruled that right to property was not part of basic structure and therefore could be suitably abridged'. The judgment's signed summary says nothing of the kind; Bhagwati J. (separate opinion) in Minerva Mills attributes the 'matter of detail' reasoning to Khanna J. alone, and the 25th Amendment's s.2(a)/(b) was upheld by the full Court on other reasoning.
value: NCERT compresses; judgment does not say this as a Court holding
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 6, Reprint 2026-27
second_source: Minerva Mills v Union of India, (1980) 3 SCC 625 / 1981 (1) SCR 206 (copy on Indian Kanoon; court copy not reached)
note: State both. Safe script wording: 'the amendments on property were upheld, and the Court did not say rights are unamendable'. The right was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (w.e.f. 20-6-1979), as NCERT p.143 also says. Audit fix 2 Nov 2026.

claim: NCERT Class XII ch.6 p.97 says in Kesavananda the Court decided there are basic features that Parliament cannot amend; p.102 says an amendment during the Emergency put the election of PM, President and Vice-President beyond court challenge.
source: NCERT Politics in India since Independence (Class XII), ch. 6, Reprint 2026-27
second_source: Constitution (Thirty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1975, Legislative Department
note: Matches the 39th Act's Statement of Objects. The 39th Amendment covers President, VP, PM and Speaker.

claim: NCERT Class VIII (Grade 8 Part 2, first edition June 2026, ch.4, p.136) says the writ and supervisory jurisdiction of the High Courts has been declared part of the basic structure of the Constitution, without naming the case.
source: NCERT Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 8 Part 2, ch. 4, First Edition June 2026
note: Not traced to a judgment; I did not read L. Chandra Kumar (1997) or other cases. Do not use on screen without a primary source.

claim: NCERT Class XI ch.6 p.127-128 and Class XII ch.6 p.97 mention the 1973 and 1975 chief-justice appointments that bypassed seniority.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 6, Reprint 2026-27
note: Not checked at primary and politically charged. Not needed for POL-06; if used, the guardrail applies (law and judgments only, no party view).

claim: NCERT Class XI p.210 says the 42nd amendment changed the Preamble, the Seventh Schedule and 53 articles.
source: NCERT Indian Constitution at Work (Class XI), ch. 9, Reprint 2026-27

claim: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 (Lok Sabha Bill No. 107 of 2026) was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 Apr 2026. As printed in the Gazette it would amend arts 55, 81, 82, 170, 330 and 332 (the House of the People to have up to 815 members from the States plus up to 35 from Union territories, and 'population' to mean the census figures Parliament decides).
source: Gazette of India Extraordinary, 16 Apr 2026, Part II Sec 2 (Lok Sabha Bill No. 107 of 2026)
page_or_section: Gazette Extraordinary, 16 Apr 2026, Part II Sec 2, Bill clauses 1-7

claim: The 131st Amendment Bill failed in the Lok Sabha on 17 Apr 2026 with 298 votes for and 230 against, short of the required two-thirds of members present and voting.
source: New India Samachar (PIB magazine), 1-15 May 2026
page_or_section: New India Samachar May 1-15, 2026 (cover story, p.14 and timeline)
note: Only a Government of India (PIB) magazine and news were seen; the Lok Sabha record (division list / debates) was not reached. The same magazine adds explanatory political text that must not be reproduced. Live example of Art. 368(2) in action; arithmetic: 2/3 of 528 present and voting would be 352, consistent with news. Needs Lok Sabha record.

claim: The Supreme Court (Sept 2026) referred a challenge to the Election Commissioners appointment law (an ordinary Act, 2023) for a larger Constitution Bench after a split between the two judges on referral. This is not a constitutional amendment, so the basic-structure doctrine is not the test.
source: Web-search summaries only (nothing read at source)
note: Seen only in web-search summaries of news (LiveLaw, SCC Online); no order read. Include only as 'what the doctrine does not apply to' if at all. Needs the Supreme Court order.

claim: No constitutional amendment has been struck down by the Supreme Court on basic-structure grounds since the NJAC judgment of 16 Oct 2015.
source: Web-search summaries only (nothing read at source)

claim: The Court's own site records that 23 Mar 1973 was the 69th day of hearing (the second last day), when Palkhivala handed in a brief submission.
source: Supreme Court of India, Basic Structure Judgment site, Arguments page (explainer, not the judgment)

claim: The Supreme Court's own explainer pages describe the case loosely (e.g. that Mutt head challenged the Act in the Kerala High Court and that the Supreme Court 'ruled in favour of the state government', and that democracy, secularism, federalism and rule of law 'cannot be amended' as if a fixed list). The judgment itself records a direct writ petition (WP 135 of 1970) in the Supreme Court, and Minerva Mills says there is no binding list.
value: explainer vs judgment: use the judgment
source: Supreme Court of India, Basic Structure Judgment site, Introduction page (explainer, not the judgment)
second_source: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala, (1973) Supp SCR 1, Supreme Court of India's own Basic Structure Judgment site
